reviews.r1Quote: "The best bánh mì I've had outside Vietnam. The baguette is perfect, the grilled pork melts, and the pickles are house-made — it makes all the difference. I come back every week."
reviews.r2Quote: "Tried the bánh xèo at lunch: the crêpe is crisp like in Saigon, the herbs ultra fresh. Quick warm service, fair prices for the quality. An exceptional neighbourhood spot."
reviews.r3Quote: "My husband is from Hanoi, and he says the cơm tấm here reminds him exactly of his mother's. Simple, clean, welcoming atmosphere. We shared the gỏi cuốn — sublime."
reviews.r4Quote: "Came for the first time after a recommendation: I wasn't disappointed. Everything is cooked to order, you can feel the respect for the ingredients. Friday bánh mì takeaway has become my ritual. Thank you HaNoiQuan!"

philosophy.h2: A clear broth, a dense memory.
philosophy.body1: Pho is not a soup. It is a memory. In Hanoi you drink it in the morning, standing on a plastic stool, in the steam of the street. At HaNoiQuan Seine we chose the Northern way: a clear, almost transparent broth where every ingredient stands out.
philosophy.body2: Beef bones, charred ginger, star anise, cinnamon, black cardamom. Twelve hours simmering, never boiling.

menu.boTaiDesc: Thin slices, just seared in the boiling broth.
menu.dacBietDesc: Every cut of beef in one bowl — rare, cooked, fat, tendons.
menu.gaDesc: Free-range chicken broth, lighter, more delicate.
menu.chayDesc: Mushroom and root vegetable broth. Not a concession, a recipe.

timeline.num: III — The broth, hour by hour
timeline.step00: Beef bones rinsed in hot water. First fire.
timeline.step02: Ginger and onions charred over high heat. Added whole.
timeline.step04: Star anise, cinnamon, black cardamom, clove. Dry-roasted, tied in muslin.
timeline.step06: The broth takes its colour. Light amber.
timeline.step09: Salt, cane sugar, fish sauce. Taste, adjust.
timeline.step12: Filtered, ready to serve. Not before.

banner.eyebrow: HaNoiQuan · House II · By the Seine
banner.title: Phở.
banner.tagline: Twelve hours of patience, one bowl per evening.
banner.imageAlt: Top-down shot of a phở bowl with rising steam — the house's signature composition.

manifesto.body1: One promise, four variations. Beef bones, ginger charred over open flame, black cardamom, cinnamon, star anise. Twelve hours simmering — never boiling. Twenty-four seats only, two services. When the broth is finished, the house closes.
manifesto.body2: In Hanoi they say a good phở is recognised by its silence. By the Seine, we decided to keep that silence.

scene.body: Bones charred in boiling water, skimmed twice. Ginger and onions burned over open flame, added whole. Star anise, black cardamom, cinnamon, clove — dry-toasted, knotted in a muslin pouch. The broth takes on its amber colour around the sixth hour. Never salted before the ninth. Strained, poured boiling. Not before.
scene.imageAlt: Full bowl of phở Sài Gòn served with fresh herbs, Thai basil and bean sprouts.

pho.title: Four compositions.
pho.dacBietDesc: Rare, cooked, fatty cuts, tendons, meatballs. Inherited from the South — the bowl that says everything in one stroke.
pho.dacBietAlt: Phở đặc biệt — every cut of beef in a single bowl.
pho.boTaiDesc: Sliced to two millimetres, laid raw on the noodles. The boiling broth does the rest.
pho.boTaiAlt: Phở bò tái — clear broth with rare beef slices.
pho.gaDesc: Free-range chicken broth. No garnish, straight to the point. Hanoi in a single spoonful.
pho.gaAlt: Phở gà in the Northern style, served without garnish.
pho.gaSudDesc: More generous with herbs. Thai basil, perilla, lime.
pho.gaSudAlt: Phở gà Saigon style, served with Thai basil and bean sprouts.

bun.title: Three bún, three Vietnams.
bun.region1Desc: The Hanoi dish, eaten by Obama and Bourdain in 2016. Charcoal-grilled pork balls and slices, rice vermicelli and herbs, dipped in a diluted nước mắm sauce.
bun.region1Why: Eat it by dipping — not mixing. The ritual matters as much as the sauce.
bun.region1Alt: Bún chả — charcoal-grilled pork, rice vermicelli and nước mắm sauce, the iconic Hanoi dish.
bun.region2Desc: The imperial soup, spicier than its cousin phở. Lemongrass, shrimp paste, chili. Deep orange broth, thick vermicelli, beef shank and pork meatballs.
bun.region2Why: In Huế they don't joke with chili. Our version stays faithful — let us know if you'd prefer it milder.
bun.region2Alt: Bún bò Huế — spicy beef and pork soup from Central Vietnam.
bun.region3Desc: Not a soup, a composed bowl. Beef sautéed with lemongrass, warm vermicelli, crushed peanuts, fried onions, herbs, sweet nước mắm sauce. Mix vigorously before the first bite.
bun.region3Why: Served dry. The broth, here, becomes sauce.
bun.region3Alt: Bún bò Nam Bộ — vermicelli, lemongrass-sautéed beef, peanuts and fresh Southern herbs.

reviews.title: What's said about us.
reviews.r1Quote: The broth is of a rare clarity. You find the rigour of Hanoi phở, the patience that no Paris menu holds anymore. Twenty-four seats, one service — it's a stance, and it's the right call.
reviews.r2Quote: Precision cooking without ostentation. The menu fits on one page, the broth simmers twelve hours, and every detail — from the charred ginger to the house chili — speaks of craft. Highly recommended.
reviews.r3Quote: I grew up with my grandmother's phở in Hà Nội. I never thought I'd find this taste in Paris — that of a broth no one rushed. The bún chả made me cry. Quietly.
reviews.r4Quote: Birthday celebrated here. Intimate evening service, warm lighting, a wildly generous bún bò Huế. Our server took time to explain each herb — that's rare. New favourite.

hero.h1: From Hanoi to Paris, by way of the kitchen.
hero.sub: One family, two houses, one way of doing things.

story.body1: It all begins in [Hanoi district], between [grandmother's / mother's] kitchen and the market. A pho broth recipe, passed down through generations.
story.body2: Arriving in Paris in [year], the family brought not a menu, but a memory. Twenty years later, two houses keep the gesture alive.
story.quote: "You don't serve a country, you serve a memory."
story.imageAlt: Chef's hands pouring pho broth into a pot, a gesture passed down through generations.

cooking.body1: Cooking Vietnamese in Paris means finding the right herbs at the market, recovering the right gesture to roll a nem, refusing the shortcuts often accepted elsewhere.
cooking.body2: We work with local producers when we can — herbs from Île-de-France, French meats — and bring from Asia what has no equivalent here: fish sauce from [origin], Northern tea, certain vegetables.

ingredients.marketBody: Fresh herbs daily, local vegetables when the season allows. Hand-picked fish sauce.
ingredients.handBody: Broth, pâté, pickles, dumplings, sauces. No industrial bases, no MSG.
ingredients.timeBody: Twelve hours for the broth. Twenty-four for the pickles. Flavour cannot be ordered, it must be waited for.
